**Alternative Datasets**  
1\. CMOSE (Comprehensive Multi-Modality Online Student Engagement)

* [CMOSE: Comprehensive Multi-Modality Online Student Engagement Dataset with High-Quality Labels](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024W/ABAW/papers/Wu_CMOSE_Comprehensive_Multi-Modality_Online_Student_Engagement_Dataset_with_High-Quality_Labels_CVPRW_2024_paper.pdf)   
* [https://huggingface.co/datasets/cwuau/CMOSE](https://huggingface.co/datasets/cwuau/CMOSE)   
* Introduced at CVPR in 2024, aims to solve data imbalance and intra-class variations found in older datasets like DAiSEE  
  * Intra-class Variations – visual, structural, numerical differences in data within the exact same category or class (want this to be as low as possible, but in human behavior is notoriously high)  
* Classifications (4 Levels)  
  * High Disengagement: 346  
  * Disengagement: 2208  
  * Engagement: 8469  
  * High Engagement: 1170  
* Includes pre extracted ground truth data (using openface)  
  * Gaze Direction and Angles  
    * Three coordinates to describe the gaze direction of left and right eyes respectively  
    * Two scalars to describe the horizontal and vertical gaze angles  
  * Head Position  
    * Three coordinates to describe the location of the head relative to the camera  
  * Head Rotation  
    * Rotation of the head described with pitch, yaw, and roll  
  * Facial Action Units (AUs)  
    * Intensities of 17 AUs represented as scalars  
    * Presence of 18 AUs represented as scalars

2\. EngageWild

* [Prediction and Localization of Student Engagement in the Wild](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8615851)   
* [https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.00858](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.00858)   
* Abhinav Dhall is also one of the authors of the EngageNet dataset  
* Focuses on "in the wild" environments with high background noise, varying illumination, and unconstrained head movement  
* 78 participants (53 males, 25 females), 19 to 27 years old  
* 195 videos, each approximately 5 minutes long, equating to about 16.5 hours of recording   
* Videos were captured in diverse, unconstrained environments including computer labs, hostel rooms, open grounds, and even simulated environments using Skype video calls to introduce network latency and varying video quality.   
* Subjects watched purely educational videos, specifically: "Learn the Korean Language in 5 minutes," a pictorial video on learning tips, and "How to write a research paper".   
* Annotators  
  * A team of 5 labelers viewed the videos with the audio turned off.   
  * Labels from reliable annotators were averaged and rounded to the nearest integer to create the final "ground truth" engagement rating for the entire 5-minute video.   
* Classifications (4 Levels)  
  * Not Engaged: 9  
  * Barely Engaged: 53  
  * Engaged: 82  
  * Highly Engaged: 50

3\. The HBCU Dataset (Cognitive Skills Training)

* [The Faces of Engagement: Automatic Recognition of Student Engagement from Facial Expressions](https://inc.ucsd.edu/mplab/46/media/EngagementRecognitionFinal.pdf)   
* 34 undergraduate students (25 females, 9 males)  
* 10,689 annotated face clips/images.  
* Classifications (4 Levels)  
  * Uses “Soft Labels,” 7 to 10 different labelers scored each clip, and their scores were averaged into a scale (if three people voted 3 and two voted 4, class \= 3.4):  
  * Not Engaged At All:  
  * Nominally Engaged:  
  * Engaged:  
  * Very Engaged:  
* Students were recorded playing an interactive "Cognitive Skills Training" game. They took a pre-test, played the game for 30 minutes, and took a post-test.

4\. Aff-Wild2 (For Transfer Learning)

* [Aff-Wild2: Extending the Aff-Wild Database for Affect Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.07770)   
* Contains 594 high-resolution YouTube videos featuring 584 subjects  
* Nearly 3 million annotated frames  
* Classifications  
  * Valence & Arousal: Continuous numerical estimation from \-1 to 1\.  
  * Expressions (8 Classes): Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happiness, Sadness, Surprise, Neutral, and "Other".  
  * Action Units (12 AUs): Specifically tracks AUs 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 15, 23, 24, 25, and 26\.  
* To gain access need to sign a EULA and email the author  
  * [https://ibug.doc.ic.ac.uk/resources/aff-wild2/](https://ibug.doc.ic.ac.uk/resources/aff-wild2/)   
  * Due to the high volume of requests, please allow about 14 days for the reply to your request for access.

**MARLIN: Masked Autoencoder for facial video Representation LearnINg**  
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.06627](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.06627) 

* The paper introduces MARLIN, a self-supervised deep learning framework designed to act as a "universal facial encoder."  
* Instead of training a neural network from scratch to do *one specific thing* (like guessing an emotion), the authors trained a model on thousands of unannotated YouTube videos to simply understand how human faces move and look.   
* Because it learns this general facial representation without needing human labels, it can be easily plugged into downstream tasks (like student engagement) as a powerful feature extractor.

* How it would be applied  
  * Instead of using OpenFace to extract features, the changepoint frames could be passed onto the pre-trained MARLIN encoder  
  * MARLIN will output a feature vector for each clip  
  * These feature vectors would be fed into the models for training
